sources.angle_name: Precision, efficiency, safety
sources.title: Building effective agents
sources.summary: Successful agents use simple composable patterns; agentic systems trade latency/cost for performance — start simple and add complexity only when measured uplift justifies it.
sources.bridge: Precision/efficiency over agent theater; reliability and cost as first-class tradeoffs.
sources.framing: The best agent teams start simple: complexity is a cost you earn with measured uplift, not a badge.

sources.angle_name: Precision, efficiency, safety
sources.title: How Small Language Models Are Key to Scalable Agentic AI
sources.summary: Most agent subtasks need narrow LLM skills; SLMs can be 10x-30x cheaper and more schema-reliable, with frontier LLMs reserved for hard reasoning in heterogeneous stacks.
sources.bridge: Right-sized models per operator step beat one giant model for everything.
sources.framing: Operators scale when every step uses the smallest model that can do the job safely.

sources.angle_name: Precision, efficiency, safety
sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.summary: NIST defines trustworthy AI (valid/reliable, safe/fail-safe, secure, accountable/transparent) and GOVERN/MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE functions for continuous risk management.
sources.bridge: Safety and reliability as engineering properties matching the precision-efficiency-safety triad.
sources.framing: Trustworthy operators are valid, fail-safe, and measurable — NIST said it before agent was a buzzword.

sources.angle_name: Precision, efficiency, safety
sources.title: In Defense of RAG in the Era of Long-Context Language Models
sources.summary: Order-preserving RAG can outperform stuffing full long contexts; quality vs chunk count forms an inverted-U; fewer well-ordered tokens can beat 100K+ dumps.
sources.bridge: Efficiency and precision: focused retrieval beats brute-force context scale.
sources.framing: More tokens isn't more intelligence — focused retrieval can beat a 100K dump.

sources.angle_name: Precision, efficiency, safety
sources.title: How to think about agent frameworks
sources.summary: Hard part of production agents is right context at each step; builder surveys cite performance quality as top blocker; hybrids of workflows and agents dominate.
sources.bridge: Reliability hinges on context control and orchestration, not abstraction layers.
sources.framing: Agent reliability is a context-engineering problem before it's a model-size problem.

sources.angle_name: Precision, efficiency, safety
sources.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach
sources.summary: Long-context can win on average when resourced, but RAG stays much cheaper; SELF-ROUTE routes via self-reflection to cut cost near LC quality.
sources.bridge: Efficiency via routing expensive long-context only when needed.
sources.framing: Route the hard queries to long context; don't tax every ticket with a million tokens.

sources.angle_name: Not conflating search with context or memory
sources.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
sources.summary: U-shaped performance: models use start/end of context best and degrade in the middle; longer windows alone do not imply robust information use.
sources.bridge: Long context is not memory; stuffing search hits into a window is not remembering.
sources.framing: A bigger context window isn't a memory system — models still get lost in the middle.

sources.angle_name: Not conflating search with context or memory
sources.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
sources.summary: OS-inspired memory hierarchy: context as RAM, external stores as disk, agent-managed paging via tools — motivated by lost-in-the-middle limits.
sources.bridge: Architecturally separates working context, recall, and archival memory from naive search-dump.
sources.framing: Context is RAM; memory is a memory hierarchy — don't conflate them.

sources.angle_name: Not conflating search with context or memory
sources.title: In Defense of RAG in the Era of Long-Context Language Models
sources.summary: Full long-context input can underperform curated retrieval; more chunks eventually add distraction and hurt answer quality.
sources.bridge: Retrieval is a distinct control surface from putting everything in context.
sources.framing: Retrieval is a decision system — not a synonym for paste the corpus.

sources.angle_name: Not conflating search with context or memory
sources.title: LaRA: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Long-Context LLMs
sources.summary: Across 2326 cases and eleven LLMs, optimal RAG vs LC depends on model, length, task, and retrieval — no silver bullet.
sources.bridge: Empirically rejects replacing RAG with long-context (or vice versa) as a slogan.
sources.framing: RAG vs long-context isn't a religion — it's a routing problem with no silver bullet.

sources.angle_name: Not conflating search with context or memory
sources.title: Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval
sources.summary: Even with perfect retrieval of evidence, longer contexts still degrade performance versus short-context settings.
sources.bridge: Separates search success from effective use of evidence in a long window.
sources.framing: Perfect retrieval still fails if you drown the model in tokens.

sources.angle_name: Not conflating search with context or memory
sources.title: Will long context replace RAG?
sources.summary: Practitioner view: RAG stays for cost, debugability, explainability; long context helps continuous reasoning; future is hybrid.
sources.bridge: Industry articulation of keeping search, context, and memory distinct.
sources.framing: If you can't explain which snippet grounded the answer, you don't have evidence — you have vibes.

sources.angle_name: Managed work to conversational work to autonomous work
sources.title: Building effective agents
sources.summary: Workflows (chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) vs agents that dynamically direct tools; escalate complexity only as needed.
sources.bridge: Managed/prescriptive paths before free-running autonomy.
sources.framing: Ship the workflow before you ship the free-running agent.

sources.angle_name: Managed work to conversational work to autonomous work
sources.title: Developing a computer use model
sources.summary: Agents act via GUI (screenshots, mouse, keyboard) with sandboxing and safety constraints — beyond chat into operating environments.
sources.bridge: Conversational systems evolving into operators that act on managed work systems.
sources.framing: Chat answers; operators act — and action needs a sandbox and a stop button.

sources.angle_name: Managed work to conversational work to autonomous work
sources.title: How to think about agent frameworks
sources.summary: Production sits on an agentic spectrum; hybrids dominate; predictability vs agency is a product choice; HITL/HOTL and persistence are first-class.
sources.bridge: Staged maturity: managed predictability, then conversational loops, then autonomy.
sources.framing: Agentic isn't binary — dial autonomy like a product setting, not a launch slogan.

sources.angle_name: Managed work to conversational work to autonomous work
sources.title: Computer-Using Agent
sources.summary: OpenAI CUA/Operator demonstrates GUI-level task execution as research preview with system-card safety framing.
sources.bridge: Industry shift from Q&A chat to task-executing operators under controls.
sources.framing: The industry just moved from answering questions to operating interfaces — governance must move with it.

sources.angle_name: Managed work to conversational work to autonomous work
sources.title: Levels of AGI for Operationalizing Progress on the Path to AGI
sources.summary: Capability levels unlock but do not mandate autonomy levels; choose Human-AI interaction paradigms by risk.
sources.bridge: Managed to autonomous is a deployment choice, not an automatic side effect of smarter models.
sources.framing: More capable models unlock higher autonomy — they don't obligate it.

sources.angle_name: Building operators; L1 to L4 autonomy
sources.title: Taxonomy and Definitions for Terms Related to Driving Automation Systems (SAE J3016)
sources.summary: Six levels (0-5) of driving automation providing shared vocabulary for human vs system responsibility.
sources.bridge: Metaphor source for L1-L4 agent autonomy messaging and shared governance language.
sources.framing: Cars got L0-L5 so insurers and regulators could talk; agents need the same clarity.

sources.angle_name: Building operators; L1 to L4 autonomy
sources.title: Levels of AGI for Operationalizing Progress on the Path to AGI
sources.summary: SAE-inspired AGI levels plus Autonomy Levels 0-5 (tool to agent); capability and autonomy treated as orthogonal.
sources.bridge: Primary academic anchor for operator levels and capability≠autonomy.
sources.framing: Capability and autonomy are orthogonal axes — don't sell L4 autonomy because you bought an L4 model.

sources.angle_name: Building operators; L1 to L4 autonomy
sources.title: Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents
sources.summary: Five user roles: operator, collaborator, consultant, approver, observer; autonomy as deliberate design; proposes autonomy certificates.
sources.bridge: Building operators is literal — climb user-role ladder deliberately.
sources.framing: Design the user's role first — operator, collaborator, approver — then set the agent's leash.

sources.angle_name: Building operators; L1 to L4 autonomy
sources.title: Leveling Up Autonomy in Agentic AI
sources.summary: CSA L0-L5 for agents with technical boundary enforcement, capability-control matrices, kill switches; L5 not advised for enterprise today.
sources.bridge: Enterprise L1-L4 operator ladder with security controls per level.
sources.framing: L3 isn't the AI is smart — it's boundaries are machine-enforced and escalation is real.

sources.angle_name: Building operators; L1 to L4 autonomy
sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.summary: AI systems operate with varying autonomy; human-AI configurations, oversight, override, and decommissioning are governance requirements.
sources.bridge: Standards language for oversight calibrated to autonomy level.
sources.framing: Oversight isn't one setting — NIST expects human-AI configurations matched to risk.

sources.angle_name: Embracing open models + safety
sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
sources.summary: Accountability/transparency, fail-safe beyond knowledge limits, appeal/override, incident response, provenance for training/decision data.
sources.bridge: Evidence management and containable failure as requirements for safe operators.
sources.framing: If you can't override, audit, and decommission it, you didn't deploy an operator — you deployed a liability.

sources.angle_name: Embracing open models + safety
sources.title: AI Act | Shaping Europe's digital future
sources.summary: Risk-based tiers (unacceptable/high/transparency/minimal); high-risk needs logging, docs, human oversight; GPAI transparency/copyright duties.
sources.bridge: Open/ecosystem models still sit in risk-tiered safety obligations.
sources.framing: Open doesn't mean ungoverned — risk tiers decide the evidence bar.

sources.angle_name: Embracing open models + safety
sources.title: Open Source Developers Guide to the EU AI Act
sources.summary: Maps Act obligations for OSS/GPAI: documentation, synthetic marking, training-data summaries, copyright opt-outs; model/dataset cards as practice.
sources.bridge: Open models with safety/documentation tooling — not open-vs-safety.
sources.framing: Open weights win when the model card, data summary, and disclosure travel with them.

sources.angle_name: Embracing open models + safety
sources.title: NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Agentic Profile
sources.summary: Tool-risk inventory including reversibility, consequence scope, auth, compositional risk; runtime metrics; autonomy-tier classification.
sources.bridge: Direct language for reversibility and evidence/telemetry in agent tool use.
sources.framing: Every tool needs a reversibility rating before you hand it to an agent.

sources.angle_name: Embracing open models + safety
sources.title: How Small Language Models Are Key to Scalable Agentic AI
sources.summary: Open Nemotron-class SLMs plus NeMo guardrails/monitoring as workhorses of heterogeneous agent stacks.
sources.bridge: Open models for controllable, fine-tunable, auditable operator steps with a safety stack.
sources.framing: Open small models + guardrails beat one opaque giant for most operator steps.

sources.angle_name: Embracing open models + safety
sources.title: Developing a computer use model
sources.summary: Computer-use training with limited software and no internet during training; safety research paired with action-taking capability.
sources.bridge: Alignment and sandboxed action as prerequisites for more autonomous operators.
sources.framing: Teach the agent to click only after you teach it where it must not click.
